doc.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Ken Burns's Jazz and the hurt to Benny Carter
summary: Jones recalls turning down Ken Burns's three-year project, which went with Stanley Crouch instead, and says the last two hours crammed in 40 people and hurt Benny Carter.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I used to be like that, because I was the hard-core, black-belt, bebop mentality, and anything that didn’t hit that thing was da-da-da-da-da, forget about it. I’m not like that. It ain’t going to be like that. Not if you can do it. If you can break – you can do anything you can when you can break out of the box, anything you’re capable of doing. I’m very proud of it. I really am, because I know in the jazz special that Ken Burns did, a lot of people were hurt. He called me first to do that. I said, “How long does it take, Ken?” He said, “Three years.” “Can’t do it.” So he went with Stanley Crouch. The last two hours covered 40 people. Benny Carter was – one of the biggest, the hurtful things that ever happened to him. He told me – he expressed it to me many times. They loped all these guys into the last two hours, and they – well, I won’t get into that, because it’s – you know what’s up.
Yeah. That was ridiculous, is what it was.
Anyway, you can’t – they can’t write me out of history, or anybody else. You can’t write Benny Carter out of history. What is, is what is. That’s somebody else’s problem.
